standard.title: Compare target language and English structures using metalanguage
standard.description: compare some target language structures and features with those of English, using some familiar metalanguage
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare text features, genre conventions and grammar patterns across target language and English using metalanguage (AC9LCH4U03). They can analyse cross-linguistic influence. They have not yet compared grammatical features systematically across different text types — active/passive voice, tense encoding, text cohesion, comparatives — or used metalanguage for text-level and grammatical analysis across multiple categories.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare structures and features of the target language and English across text types and grammatical categories, using metalanguage — including text organisation, grammar rules, voice, tense encoding, and cohesive devices.

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical features across languages
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare specific grammatical features across the target language and English — including voice, tense encoding, comparative structures, and adjectival functions — using metalanguage.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two grammatical features across the target language and English using metalanguage, explaining where the features work similarly and where they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Compare passive and active voice across target language and English; compare tense encoding (conjugation versus time expressions); compare comparative and superlative structures; explore adjectival verb constructions; use metalanguage from both languages to describe grammatical rules.
wider: Investigate a grammatical feature that exists in the target language but not in English (or vice versa) — explain what communicative function it serves and how the other language handles the same communicative need
Create a bilingual grammar comparison resource — explaining a specific grammatical contrast to a student learning one of the two languages
nodes.hinge_reason: Grammatical comparison using metalanguage is the prerequisite for all analytical text work at this level. Students who cannot describe grammatical differences using metalanguage cannot analyse texts, explain language choices, or support their own writing decisions with linguistic reasoning.

response_modes.reason: Grammatical comparison requires students to hold two systems in mind simultaneously and reason about structural differences. Explicit comparison frames and systematic category-by-category analysis build the analytical capacity before students can compare independently.

success_criteria: Compares at least two grammatical features across target language and English using metalanguage
Explains for each feature where the two languages work similarly and where they differ

nodes.label: Comparing text types and cohesive conventions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare structural features, language conventions and cohesive devices across text types in the target language and English.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare the structural features of the same text type (e.g. a narrative, a procedure, a recount) in target language and English, identifying at least three differences.
nodes.typical_width: Compare features of different text types across target language and English — descriptive language in narratives, persuasive language in advertisements, procedural structure; compare audience and purpose conventions; explore how cohesive devices function differently across the two languages.
wider: Analyse the cohesive devices used in a target language text and compare with an equivalent English text — identify where the cohesion strategy is similar and where it requires a different approach
Compare how imperatives function in instruction texts across target language and English — identify differences in directness, politeness marking, and structural conventions

response_modes.reason: Text type comparison across languages requires encounter with varied text types — students who have only compared narratives cannot generalise their comparative strategies to procedures, recounts or persuasive texts. Varied text type comparison builds flexible analytical capacity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Text comparison across languages develops the bilingual analytical lens that is a distinctive competence of background language learners. Width investment here — particularly in comparing texts the student encounters in real life (advertising, news, digital communication) — makes the analysis genuinely relevant.
success_criteria: Identifies at least three structural or cohesive differences between the same text type in target language and English
Can explain how at least one cohesive device functions differently across the two languages

nodes.label: Creating comparative analyses using metalanguage
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can produce a structured language comparison — written or presented — using metalanguage to explain patterns of similarity and difference across the target language and English.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce a structured comparison of at least two language features using metalanguage, with examples from both languages.
nodes.typical_width: Create comparative vocabulary lists, annotated text analyses, or structured presentations comparing language features; use metalanguage from both languages; discuss how language features across the two systems reflect different ways of organising meaning.
wider: Create a structured metalinguistic analysis of a target language text — annotate every grammatical and textual feature using metalanguage, then compare with an English equivalent annotation
Present a language comparison to peers as an explanation task — requiring the student to make the analysis accessible and accurate for an audience who may not know both languages

response_modes.reason: Producing a comparative analysis integrates grammatical comparison (node 1) and text type awareness (node 2) into a full metalinguistic task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine comparison contexts — real texts, real linguistic questions — that make the analysis meaningful rather than mechanical.

success_criteria: Produces a comparison of at least two language features using metalanguage with examples from both languages
The comparison is accurate and clearly organised for a reader
